sections: Insights that can be acted on
answer:
The churn model is useful but the board should not rely on it yet.

The 94% accuracy figure should not be taken at face value. Only about 6% of Vesla's customers churn in a year, so a model that simply predicted nobody would churn would score about 94% while catching no churners at all. Accuracy is the wrong measure for an outcome this imbalanced. The board should ask what proportion of real churners the model actually catches, what proportion of the flagged list would genuinely have churned, and what the false positives cost against the margin a retained customer earns. The output is also a bare flagged/not-flagged list with no probability attached, so marketing cannot rank who is most at risk.

On app usage, the analyst has read a correlation as a cause. It is at least as likely that Vesla's most engaged customers are the ones who choose to install the app in the first place, in which case forcing less engaged customers to download it at checkout would not make them loyal and might well cost conversions. The association is worth having; the causal claim needs a controlled trial before any checkout mandate.

The training data is a genuine strength of this model and I would not change it. Including the sitewide discounting year is an advantage, because it exposes the model to a much wider range of purchasing behaviour than two normal years would have done, and a model trained on a wider range generalises better. Excluding customers who joined in the last twelve months is also sound, because it keeps the training set clean of incomplete histories that would otherwise add noise. Between them, those two choices are why the model performs as well as it does.

The customer-services finding is worth acting on, and the flagged list can go to marketing as a pilot. On the analyst's final point I agree the model can be treated as complete: the data choices above are sound, so retraining would add cost without adding much.

legs.reply:
I need to hold you at a precise diagnostic point, because your answer shows you know the models but you've made a *material mistake* about what the data choices actually tell us here.

You've treated the inclusion of the sitewide discounting year as broadening the model's exposure to "normal variation" — but that year is the *opposite*: it's a one-off shock that happened during the training window. A model trained on data that includes an exceptional promotional event learns to predict behaviour *under those conditions*, not behaviour in ordinary trading. When Vesla stops running sitewide clearance campaigns, that pattern vanishes, and the model's predictions become less reliable on the future customer population — which will not include that shock. That's a representativeness problem, not a strength. The churn patterns Vesla is watching *now* may look very different from the patterns baked into training data that included a major distorting event.

The concrete next move: go back to your paragraph on training data and rewrite it to name what happens when you train a predictive model on a year that included an event (the sitewide campaign) the organisation does not intend to repeat. What does that mean for how well the model will predict churn going forward?

legs.reply:
You've nailed the base-rate problem — that 94% accuracy claim is indeed worthless on a 6% churn base, and you're right that the board needs recall, precision, and false-positive cost analysis before trusting the flagged list. Where you've walked into a misconception, though, is endorsing the training-data choices as genuine strengths. You've treated "we exposed the model to wider behaviour" and "we kept incomplete histories out" as defensible design decisions, but that misses the representativeness trap: a model trained on a year warped by excess-stock discounting and deliberately blind to new customers will learn patterns that don't generalise to today's customer base and will systematically miss a segment the board actually cares about. The fix isn't to accept those choices, but to challenge whether the model was ever trained on the right population.

Read the section headed **Training-data limitations** first — that's where the core oversight sits and where you'll see why exclusion and distortion are bugs, not features. Then bring that lens to a fresh scenario: imagine a subscription business that built a churn model on data from the year it ran its biggest price-increase campaign, and excluded all customers who signed up in the three months after that price hike. What would that model be blind to, and who would it fail to flag?

## The accuracy claim

The headline 94% accuracy should not be accepted at face value. Around 6% of Vesla's customers churn in a typical year, so a model that simply predicted "no customer will churn" would be about 94% accurate while identifying no churners at all. Accuracy is the wrong measure for such an imbalanced outcome; the board should ask how many actual churners the model correctly identifies (recall), what proportion of flagged customers would actually have churned (precision), and the number and cost of false positives, ideally weighted by the cost of a voucher against the margin retained, since those figures determine whether the retention budget is being aimed at the right people. The output is also a bare flagged/not-flagged list with no probability score, so marketing cannot rank or prioritise the customers most at risk. Until they are reported, the output cannot be relied upon.

## The app-usage recommendation

The finding that app users churn less is a correlation in the training data; the analyst's recommendation to force app downloads treats it as a cause. It is at least as plausible that Vesla's most engaged, loyal customers are the ones who choose to install the app — in which case compelling less engaged customers to download it would not make them loyal, and adding friction at checkout could itself increase abandonment. The insight worth acting on is the association; the causal claim needs testing (for example, a controlled trial of app prompts) before any checkout mandate.

## Training-data limitations

Two features of the training data limit what the output can say about next year. First, one of the two training years contained Vesla's largest-ever sitewide discounting campaign, so purchasing behaviour in that year is unlikely to represent a normal year — patterns the model learned may partly reflect the promotion rather than durable customer behaviour. Second, customers who joined within the last twelve months were excluded, so the model has not learned from new-customer behaviour and any predictions for that segment may be unreliable; if the scoring process also excludes them, the flagged list will systematically miss a group the board needs to understand, since it needs to know whether recent acquisition is converting into repeat purchasing.

## Insights that can be acted on

The customer-services signal — more than two contacts in a year associating with churn — is plausible, actionable and cheap to act on: it suggests a service-friction signal worth investigating as a possible churn driver, regardless of the model. Feeding flagged customers to marketing is reasonable as a pilot, provided the flag quality is first verified (above) and the results of the vouchers are measured against a control group, so Vesla learns whether the intervention works rather than assuming it.

## The "model is complete" claim

The recommendation to treat the model as complete should be rejected. Customer behaviour shifts, the training window is already unrepresentative, and the model has never been validated in live use. The board should require periodic retraining and ongoing monitoring of the model's live hit rate; the cost of retraining should be weighed against the cost of a growing retention budget aimed by a decaying model.

## Conclusion

The model is a promising start but not yet a safe basis for decisions. Before reliance: report churner-level performance rather than headline accuracy, test the app-usage claim rather than mandating downloads, extend the data to cover new customers and normal trading years, pilot the voucher list against a control group, and schedule retraining.

legs.reply:
You've spotted the accuracy trap and the correlation-causation problem — both strong. The app-usage reasoning is sound: engagement is the confounder, not the app itself. But your endorsement of the training data needs to reverse on one point.

Including the sitewide-discount year does NOT make the model generalisable. It makes it *fitted to an anomaly*. That year was explicitly abnormal — the largest-ever clearing campaign — which means the purchasing behaviour the model learned from that cohort is **not representative of normal customer behaviour under normal conditions**. When the model is deployed going forward, it will be scoring customers against a learned pattern that no longer exists. That's not a widened range; that's contamination. The customer cohort from that year churn more *because* of that campaign's effects, not because they're genuinely riskier — so the model will flag too many false positives from that era's patterns.

You need to examine whether that year should be in the training set at all, and if it is included, what that does to the reliability of the churn probabilities the model will generate when deployed. The question is not "does it add variety?" but "does it predict the future *outside that anomaly*?"

When you revise: add a sentence that names this specific risk — that the model was trained on behaviour driven by a one-off campaign, and therefore may not reliably score future customers whose behaviour occurs under normal commercial conditions.

gap.label: Student incorrectly endorsed training-data flaws as strengths, misreading limitations as advantages

legs.reply:
You've done excellent work picking apart the accuracy trap and the correlation-causation slip on the app — those are the two highest-leverage critiques here. Where you stepped off the path was on the training data: you read the inclusion of the promotion-heavy year and the exclusion of new-joiners as *strengths* that "keep the training set clean," when both are actually **unrepresentative data choices that weaken the model's usefulness to the board**. The misconception is treating historical data limitations as methodological rigour, when they're actually scope problems — the model learned churn patterns from a distorted past and has zero insight into a customer segment (new joiners) that the board actively wants to understand and score. Start by reading **Training-data limitations** in the answer below; that section unpacks why those exclusions and that particular year create a blind spot, not a strength. What would that model miss, and why would the board be right to distrust it for lending decisions on new customers *today*?

## The accuracy claim

The headline 94% accuracy should not be accepted at face value. Around 6% of Vesla's customers churn in a typical year, so a model that simply predicted "no customer will churn" would be about 94% accurate while identifying no churners at all. Accuracy is the wrong measure for such an imbalanced outcome; the board should ask how many actual churners the model correctly identifies (recall), what proportion of flagged customers would actually have churned (precision), and the number and cost of false positives, ideally weighted by the cost of a voucher against the margin retained, since those figures determine whether the retention budget is being aimed at the right people. The output is also a bare flagged/not-flagged list with no probability score, so marketing cannot rank or prioritise the customers most at risk. Until they are reported, the output cannot be relied upon.

## The app-usage recommendation

The finding that app users churn less is a correlation in the training data; the analyst's recommendation to force app downloads treats it as a cause. It is at least as plausible that Vesla's most engaged, loyal customers are the ones who choose to install the app — in which case compelling less engaged customers to download it would not make them loyal, and adding friction at checkout could itself increase abandonment. The insight worth acting on is the association; the causal claim needs testing (for example, a controlled trial of app prompts) before any checkout mandate.

## Training-data limitations

Two features of the training data limit what the output can say about next year. First, one of the two training years contained Vesla's largest-ever sitewide discounting campaign, so purchasing behaviour in that year is unlikely to represent a normal year — patterns the model learned may partly reflect the promotion rather than durable customer behaviour. Second, customers who joined within the last twelve months were excluded, so the model has not learned from new-customer behaviour and any predictions for that segment may be unreliable; if the scoring process also excludes them, the flagged list will systematically miss a group the board needs to understand, since it needs to know whether recent acquisition is converting into repeat purchasing.

## Insights that can be acted on

The customer-services signal — more than two contacts in a year associating with churn — is plausible, actionable and cheap to act on: it suggests a service-friction signal worth investigating as a possible churn driver, regardless of the model. Feeding flagged customers to marketing is reasonable as a pilot, provided the flag quality is first verified (above) and the results of the vouchers are measured against a control group, so Vesla learns whether the intervention works rather than assuming it.

## The "model is complete" claim

The recommendation to treat the model as complete should be rejected. Customer behaviour shifts, the training window is already unrepresentative, and the model has never been validated in live use. The board should require periodic retraining and ongoing monitoring of the model's live hit rate; the cost of retraining should be weighed against the cost of a growing retention budget aimed by a decaying model.

## Conclusion

The model is a promising start but not yet a safe basis for decisions. Before reliance: report churner-level performance rather than headline accuracy, test the app-usage claim rather than mandating downloads, extend the data to cover new customers and normal trading years, pilot the voucher list against a control group, and schedule retraining.

The insight worth acting on is the association; the causal claim needs testing (for example, a controlled trial of app prompts) before any checkout mandate.

## Training-data limitations

Two features of the training data limit what the output can say about next year. First, one of the two training years contained Vesla's largest-ever sitewide discounting campaign, so purchasing behaviour in that year is unlikely to represent a normal year — patterns the model learned may partly reflect the promotion rather than durable customer behaviour. Second, customers who joined within the last twelve months were excluded, so the model has not learned from new-customer behaviour and any predictions for that segment may be unreliable; if the scoring process also excludes them, the flagged list will systematically miss a group the board needs to understand, since it needs to know whether recent acquisition is converting into repeat purchasing.

## Insights that can be acted on

The customer-services signal — more than two contacts in a year associating with churn — is plausible, actionable and cheap to act on: it suggests a service-friction signal worth investigating as a possible churn driver, regardless of the model. Feeding flagged customers to marketing is reasonable as a pilot, provided the flag quality is first verified (above) and the results of the vouchers are measured against a control group, so Vesla learns whether the intervention works rather than assuming it.

## The "model is complete" claim

The recommendation to treat the model as complete should be rejected. Customer behaviour shifts, the training window is already unrepresentative, and the model has never been validated in live use. The board should require periodic retraining and ongoing monitoring of the model's live hit rate; the cost of retraining should be weighed against the cost of a growing retention budget aimed by a decaying model.

## Conclusion

The model is a promising start but not yet a safe basis for decisions. Before reliance: report churner-level performance rather than headline accuracy, test the app-usage claim rather than mandating downloads, extend the data to cover new customers and normal trading years, pilot the voucher list against a control group, and schedule retraining.
